# 0. Purpose of this notebook

Study 1 tests whether the source attribution of an artwork (AI vs. Human)
is enough by itself to change how lay viewers judge it. Nothing else is
manipulated: there is no modification, no derivative step and no information
about time invested. Participants judge two things. **Creativity** stands for
the minimal spark of creativity that *Feist* requires for copyright. **Effort**
stands for sweat of the brow, the view that labor alone earns protection,
which *Feist* rejected and which Allen invoked on appeal. Study 1 is the
baseline. It shows whether the "original sin" bias is present at the first
step of the copyright evaluation, before anything has been done to the work.
Studies 2–5 then test whether modification, disclosure of effort, or the two
together can rescue a source attributed to AI.

**Design.** 2 (Creator Type: AI vs. Human, between-subjects, so each
participant sees one label) × 2 (Stimulus Type: Figure vs. NonFigure,
within-subjects, so each participant sees both kinds). Each participant rates
10 source artworks, five that contain a figure and five that do not, on two
5-point Likert scales (Creativity, Effort), and writes a justification for
each rating. That gives 10 × 2 = 20 ratings and 20 open-ended responses per
participant.

**What this notebook produces.**

1. The exclusion flow, which yields the analytic sample. Exclusion rules were
   fixed before analysis; Study 1 was **not** prospectively preregistered. A
   secondary-analysis registration (2026) covers the joint model (§7.6),
   maximal random effects (§7.5), diagnostics (§7.7), the registered
   effect-size convention (§9.1) and the computational text program
   (`Study1_02_Text.ipynb`).
2. A long-format data frame with one row per participant, stimulus and
   dimension. It feeds the mixed-effects analyses below and is the input file
   for the companion text-analysis notebook (`Study1_02_Text.ipynb`).
3. The primary results, from linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) with crossed
   random effects for participants and stimuli: each participant and each
   image gets its own baseline, and every participant rates every image.
4. Robustness checks with cumulative-link mixed models (CLMMs), which treat
   the five Likert responses as ordered categories rather than as equally
   spaced numbers.
5. Welch *t*-tests (*t*-tests that do not assume equal variances in the two
   arms) on participant averages, which repeat the analysis in the earlier
   report, and the single registered Cohen's *d* convention (§9.1).
6. The fully maximal random-effects model (§7.5), the joint model of both
   dimensions that tests the comparative claim (§7.6), and the assumption
   and influence diagnostics (§7.7).
7. The registered tests of H4 (§7.8) and H3 (§7.10), the Holm correction (a
   stepwise adjustment for testing several hypotheses together) across the
   confirmatory family (§7.9), and a sensitivity check on one
   differently worded item (§7.11).
8. Per-image sensitivity analyses, drawn as forest plots (one estimate and
   interval per image), that show whether any single image drives the
   headline effect.
9. Figures and statistics tables (`.csv`) for the LaTeX manuscript.

# 1. Setup

## 1.1 Packages

```{r packages, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core tidyverse and statistics packages, each with a note on what it is
# used for here.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)   # pipes, dplyr, tidyr, ggplot2, readr, purrr
library(here)        # path handling that survives working-directory changes
library(janitor)     # clean_names(), tabyl(), adorn_*() for quick crosstabs

# Mixed-effects models. lme4 fits the models. lmerTest wraps lme4 so that
# summary() and anova() return p-values with Satterthwaite degrees of
# freedom, an approximation to the degrees of freedom a test in a mixed model
# effectively has. Satterthwaite degrees of freedom are the usual choice in
# psychology, and Studies 2-5 will use them as well, so the studies stay
# comparable.
library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)

# emmeans gives estimated marginal means (model-based cell means) and the
# contrasts between them on the LMM fits, with a Tukey adjustment for the
# number of comparisons where one is asked for, and a Cohen's d for each
# contrast through eff_size(). That d divides by the residual standard
# deviation only; section 9.1 explains why it is not the registered d.
library(emmeans)

# Effect sizes and model diagnostics. performance::r2() gives the marginal
# R^2 (variance explained by the fixed effects alone) and the conditional R^2
# (fixed and random effects together), following Nakagawa and Schielzeth.
# effectsize::eta_squared() gives partial eta^2, the share of variance an
# effect accounts for out of that effect plus error, for the ANOVA tables.
library(performance)
library(effectsize)

# Ordinal robustness check. A Likert rating is an ordered category, not a
# measured quantity, and reviewers often object to treating 1-5 as
# continuous. clmm() fits a cumulative-link mixed model, which estimates
# where the cut points between adjacent ratings fall instead of assuming they
# are evenly spaced. If the LMM and the CLMM agree on direction and
# significance, treating the ratings as continuous is defensible. The LMM
# leads because its coefficients are in rating points; the CLMM goes in the
# supplement.
library(ordinal)

# broom and broom.mixed turn model objects into data frames with one row per
# estimate, the shape the CSV tables and the paper tables are written from.
library(broom)
library(broom.mixed)

# Figures. ggpubr supplies the violin, box and jitter style used for Studies
# 2-5, which these figures match. patchwork assembles multi-panel figures.
# scales formats the axes.
library(ggpubr)
library(patchwork)
library(scales)

# sessionInfo() is printed at the end. The seed is set here so that any
# random step that does not set its own seed is reproducible.
set.seed(20260421)
```

## 1.2 Paths & config

```{r paths-config}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Project layout on Google Drive (macOS File Stream for Drive):
#
#   DGK Lab - Copyrightability and AI Art/
#   ├── Data/
#   │   ├── Study 1/                     <- raw Qualtrics CSVs live here
#   │   │   ├── Study1_Values.csv        <- numeric-coded export (ratings)
#   │   │   └── Study1_Labels.csv        <- label-coded export (text + demog.)
#   │   ├── Study 2/  ... Study 5/
#   ├── Analysis/
#   │   └── R Analysis Pipeline/
#   │       ├── Study 1/                 <- analysis files + outputs live here
#   │       │   ├── Study1_01_Quant.Rmd  <- this file
#   │       │   ├── Study1_02_Text.ipynb
#   │       │   ├── Study1_03_Integration.Rmd
#   │       │   ├── tables/   figures/   models/   nlp/
#   │       └── Study 2/ ... Study 5/
#   └── Docs/
#       └── Writing/
#           └── Final Paper/             <- manuscript + paper-ready outputs
#               ├── tables/              <- LaTeX \input-able fragments
#               └── figures/             <- publication-grade figures
#
# PROJECT_ROOT below is found from this file's own folder, which is the
# working directory when the file is knitted: it is the first folder at or
# above it that holds both Data and Analysis. The environment variable
# STUDY1_PROJECT_ROOT, when set, names the root instead, as
# STUDY2_PROJECT_ROOT to STUDY5_PROJECT_ROOT do for the other studies. Every
# other path is built from it. The path contains spaces, which R handles as
# long as paths are built with file.path() and not by pasting strings
# together.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

PROJECT_ROOT <- local({
  is_root <- function(p) dir.exists(file.path(p, "Data")) &&
                         dir.exists(file.path(p, "Analysis"))
  root <- Sys.getenv("STUDY1_PROJECT_ROOT")
  if (nzchar(root)) {
    root <- normalizePath(root, mustWork = FALSE)
    if (!is_root(root)) {
      stop("The folder STUDY1_PROJECT_ROOT names has no Data and Analysis ",
           "folders.")
    }
  } else {
    root <- normalizePath(getwd(), mustWork = TRUE)
    while (!is_root(root)) {
      if (identical(dirname(root), root)) {
        stop("No folder at or above the working directory holds both Data ",
             "and Analysis. Knit this file from its own folder, or set ",
             "STUDY1_PROJECT_ROOT to the project root.")
      }
      root <- dirname(root)
    }
  }
  root
})

# Per-study identifiers. When this file is copied for Studies 2-5, only this
# block needs to change, along with the rating and response column patterns
# further down, which differ across studies.

# Data (raw Qualtrics exports)
PATH_DATA        <- file.path(PROJECT_ROOT, "Data", STUDY_FOLDER)
PATH_DATA_VALUES <- file.path(PATH_DATA, "Study1_Values.csv")
PATH_DATA_LABELS <- file.path(PATH_DATA, "Study1_Labels.csv")

# Analysis folder (this .Rmd lives here; outputs go here too)
PATH_ANALYSIS    <- file.path(PROJECT_ROOT, "Analysis",
                              "R Analysis Pipeline", STUDY_FOLDER)
PATH_OUT         <- PATH_ANALYSIS              # outputs sit alongside the .Rmd
PATH_OUT_FIG     <- file.path(PATH_OUT, "figures")

# Paper-ready outputs (LaTeX fragments + publication figures)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Greyscale palette. It avoids red and green, which readers with

PALETTE_TYPE <- c("Human" = "#A1A1A1", "AI" = "#3E3E3E")
```

```{r run-record}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Run record. Every file this notebook writes is tied to one run of it.
#
#   RUN_START     the clock time at which this run began. The manifest written
#                 at the end of section 13 compares each output's
#                 modification time against it, so a file that this run did
#                 not write reads as not written this run.
#   INPUT_SHA256  the SHA-256 checksum of each input file, a 64-character
#                 fingerprint of the file's exact bytes that changes if any
#                 byte of the file changes. This notebook reads two inputs,
#                 the two Qualtrics exports.
#   RUN_ID        the start time followed by the first eight characters of a
#                 checksum taken over the input checksums, so two runs on the
#                 same exports share the suffix and a run on different exports
#                 does not.
#
# The previous run's manifest is deleted here, before anything else is
# written. A run that stops part way therefore leaves no manifest, and a file
# downstream that requires one cannot take a half-finished set of outputs for
# a finished one.
#
# clear_outputs() is called at the top of every chunk that writes a file. It
# deletes that chunk's outputs from the previous run before the chunk computes
# anything, so a chunk that fails leaves its files missing rather than leaving
# the previous run's copies in place, and it adds each path to QUANT_OUTPUTS,
# the list the manifest is built from.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
RUN_START <- Sys.time()

INPUT_FILES <- c(values_export = PATH_DATA_VALUES,
                 labels_export = PATH_DATA_LABELS)
stopifnot(all(file.exists(INPUT_FILES)))
INPUT_SHA256 <- unname(tools::sha256sum(INPUT_FILES))

# tools::sha256sum() reads files, so the checksum over the input checksums is
# taken on a temporary file holding them one per line.
input_hash_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".txt")
writeLines(INPUT_SHA256, input_hash_file)
RUN_ID <- paste0(format(RUN_START, "%Y%m%dT%H%M%S"), "-",
                 substr(unname(tools::sha256sum(input_hash_file)), 1, 8))
unlink(input_hash_file)

PATH_RUN_MANIFEST <- file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_quant_run_manifest.csv")
PATH_RUN_INPUTS   <- file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_quant_run_inputs.csv")
unlink(PATH_RUN_MANIFEST)

QUANT_OUTPUTS <- character(0)
clear_outputs <- function(...) {
  paths <- c(...)
  QUANT_OUTPUTS <<- union(QUANT_OUTPUTS, paths)
  unlink(paths)
  invisible(paths)
}

# The input record: one row per input file, with its checksum and size.
clear_outputs(PATH_RUN_INPUTS)
run_inputs <- tibble(run_id = RUN_ID,
                     input  = names(INPUT_FILES),
                     file   = basename(INPUT_FILES),
                     bytes  = unname(file.size(INPUT_FILES)),
                     sha256 = INPUT_SHA256)
write_csv(run_inputs, PATH_RUN_INPUTS)

cat("RUN_ID =", RUN_ID, "\n")
print(as.data.frame(run_inputs %>% select(input, file, bytes, sha256)))
```

## 1.3 Likert-response coding

```{r likert-coding}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The ratings come from Values.csv, which carries Qualtrics's numeric codes
# (1-5), not from the label text. The label text is not
# the same on every item, so a mapping from labels to numbers would have to be
# written item by item; the numeric codes are what each participant actually
# selected and need no mapping.
#
# The anchors differ on one item. In the survey definition file
# (qualtrics/Final_-_AI_Copyright_-_Study_1.qsf, question QID363) the effort
# question for the first figurative image, 1FigureEff, offers
#   4 = "A lot of effort involved", 5 = "Significant effort involved";
# the other nine effort items offer
#   4 = "Significant effort involved", 5 = "A great deal of effort involved".
# So "Significant effort involved" is a 5 on 1FigureEff and a 4 everywhere
# else, and that item has no "A great deal of effort involved" option at all.
# The item is scored as answered; section 7.11 refits the registered effort
# quantities without it to show how much it matters.
#
# This mapping is documentation only: it records what each number means on
# the nineteen items that share these anchors.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
LIKERT_LABELS <- tribble(
  ~dimension,   ~value, ~label,
  "creativity",  1,     "No creativity involved",
  "creativity",  2,     "Minimal creativity involved",
  "creativity",  3,     "Moderate creativity involved",
  "creativity",  4,     "Significant creativity involved",
  "creativity",  5,     "A great deal of creativity involved",
  "effort",      1,     "No effort involved",
  "effort",      2,     "Minimal effort involved",
  "effort",      3,     "Moderate effort involved",
  "effort",      4,     "Significant effort involved",   # "A lot of effort involved" on 1FigureEff
  "effort",      5,     "A great deal of effort involved" # "Significant effort involved" on 1FigureEff
)
LIKERT_LABELS
```

# 2. Data ingestion

## 2.1 Load raw Qualtrics exports

```{r load-raw, message=FALSE}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Qualtrics CSV exports have two metadata rows between the header and the
# first data row:
#   Row 1: variable names (the header kept here)
#   Row 2: human-readable question text (the full prompt)
#   Row 3: Qualtrics ImportID JSON metadata
# The header is read on its own first. The data are then read with skip = 3,
# which passes over the header and both metadata rows, and the saved header
# is attached. skip on its own would drop the header with the metadata rows.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
raw_header <- read_csv(
  PATH_DATA_VALUES,
  n_max          = 0,                  # read header only
  show_col_types = FALSE
) %>% colnames()

# Read the data, skipping the 3 header rows, and attach the saved header.
# col_types = cols(.default = "c") reads every column as text, and columns
# are converted to numbers or factors explicitly later. Letting readr guess
# is less safe: it misreads the rating columns, because the first row
# happens to have missing values.
raw_values <- read_csv(
  PATH_DATA_VALUES,
  skip           = 3,
  col_names      = raw_header,
  col_types      = cols(.default = "c"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Also load the Labels export. It supplies the fields that read better as
# text (condition, demographics such as Gender, Race, Language and
# Experience, and the exclusion items) and the written justifications. The
# ratings themselves come from Values.csv.
raw_labels <- read_csv(
  PATH_DATA_LABELS,
  skip           = 3,
  col_names      = read_csv(PATH_DATA_LABELS, n_max = 0,
                            show_col_types = FALSE) %>% colnames(),
  col_types      = cols(.default = "c"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Both exports should have the same number of rows, one per Qualtrics
# response record. If they do not, check the export filter settings.
stopifnot(nrow(raw_values) == nrow(raw_labels))

cat("Loaded", nrow(raw_values), "records x", ncol(raw_values), "columns.\n")
```

## 2.2 Build a working frame

```{r build-working-frame}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# One "working" data frame combines the numeric ratings from Values.csv with
# the text justifications and demographics from Labels.csv. Only the columns
# needed are selected, which drops the dozens of per-page timing variables
# Qualtrics exports (kept for a later engagement check, not needed for the
# primary analyses).
#
# Column-name convention in the raw data:
#   {stimulusNum}{stimulusType}{dimension}        e.g., 3FigureCreat
#   {stimulusNum}{stimulusType}{dimension}Resp    e.g., 3FigureCreatResp
# where stimulusNum in {1,2,3,4,5}, stimulusType in {Figure, NonFigure},
# dimension in {Creat, Eff}. That gives 10 stimuli * 2 dimensions = 20 rating
# columns and 20 response-text columns, 40 item-level columns per participant.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Find the item-level columns by a regular expression on the column names.
rating_cols <- grep("^\\d+(Figure|NonFigure)(Creat|Eff)$",
                    names(raw_values), value = TRUE)
resp_cols   <- grep("^\\d+(Figure|NonFigure)(Creat|Eff)Resp$",
                    names(raw_values), value = TRUE)

cat("Found", length(rating_cols), "rating columns and",
    length(resp_cols), "response-text columns.\n")
stopifnot(length(rating_cols) == 20, length(resp_cols) == 20)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Join key: `ResponseId`, not `id`.
#
# `id` is the subject-pool identifier the participant typed in, not
# Qualtrics's record key. The two "Survey Preview" test records in the
# export have id == NA. dplyr's default `na_matches = "na"` treats NA as
# equal to NA, so a join keyed on `id` would match each NA-id row in
# meta_block to both NA-id rows in ratings_block (2 x 2 = 4) and then to both
# in responses_block (4 x 2 = 8), fabricating records that never existed.
#
# So the join is keyed on `ResponseId`, Qualtrics's own record id, which is
# in both exports and is never NA or duplicated. The join declares the
# expected cardinality, meaning how many rows on each side may match
# (`relationship = "one-to-one"`), so dplyr stops with an error rather than
# silently multiplying rows. It also sets `na_matches = "never"`, so an NA key
# matches nothing. Assertions right after the join state the invariants, the
# conditions that must hold for the join to be trusted.
# Participant `id` stays the key downstream (models, long frame, text
# notebook). Its own invariants are asserted in §3 after the preview records
# are removed, because the preview rows are the only ones with NA id.
#
# For the Studies 2-5 template: any Qualtrics export can contain preview or
# test rows with a blank participant id, so the template must (a) key on
# ResponseId, (b) filter on Status and (c) assert cardinality, in that order.
# Never join on a participant-typed id before the preview filter.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Structural pre-checks: the join key must exist in both exports and be a
# unique, non-missing identifier in each.
stopifnot(
  "ResponseId" %in% names(raw_values),
  "ResponseId" %in% names(raw_labels),
  !anyNA(raw_values$ResponseId),
  !anyNA(raw_labels$ResponseId),
  !any(duplicated(raw_values$ResponseId)),
  !any(duplicated(raw_labels$ResponseId)),
  setequal(raw_values$ResponseId, raw_labels$ResponseId)
)

# The participant id must agree between the two exports record-by-record
# (they are two renderings of the same Qualtrics response set). NA == NA is
# allowed here only for the preview rows; §3 removes those.
id_xwalk <- raw_values %>%
  select(ResponseId, id_values = id) %>%
  inner_join(raw_labels %>% select(ResponseId, id_labels = id),
             by = "ResponseId", relationship = "one-to-one")
stopifnot(
  nrow(id_xwalk) == nrow(raw_values),
  all((id_xwalk$id_values == id_xwalk$id_labels) |
      (is.na(id_xwalk$id_values) & is.na(id_xwalk$id_labels)))
)

# Every rating cell must be blank or a whole number from 1 to 5. as.integer()
# below would truncate a value such as "3.5" to 3 and turn stray text into NA
# without stopping, so the raw strings are checked before it runs.
raw_rating_cells <- unlist(raw_values[rating_cols], use.names = FALSE)
bad_rating_cells <- !is.na(raw_rating_cells) & raw_rating_cells != "" &
  !grepl("^[1-5]$", raw_rating_cells)
if (any(bad_rating_cells)) {
  stop(sum(bad_rating_cells), " rating cell(s) in Study1_Values.csv are not ",
       "a whole number from 1 to 5: ",
       paste(head(unique(raw_rating_cells[bad_rating_cells]), 10),
             collapse = ", "))
}

# Assemble the numeric-rating block (from Values) and the text-response block
# (from Labels), each keyed on ResponseId. `id` is carried only in meta_block
# so the join cannot produce id.x / id.y duplicates.
ratings_block  <- raw_values %>%
  select(ResponseId, all_of(rating_cols)) %>%
  # Coerce ratings to numeric here, once, so downstream code never has to
  # re-parse them.
  mutate(across(all_of(rating_cols), as.integer))

responses_block <- raw_labels %>%
  select(ResponseId, all_of(resp_cols))

# Metadata (Type, demographics, exclusion fields) are read from Labels,
# where they appear as text. Progress and Duration are numeric and are
# converted explicitly.
# ResponseId, Status and DistributionChannel are carried so §3 can drop
# Qualtrics preview records by their documented flag rather than by the
# accident of a missing id. In the Labels export Status is the text
# "IP Address" / "Survey Preview" (Values codes the same field 0 / 1).
meta_block <- raw_labels %>%
  select(ResponseId, Status, DistributionChannel,
         id, Progress, Finished, `Duration (in seconds)`,
         Type, ConsentForm, AttentionCheck, Seriousness,
         Race, Gender, Age, Language, Experience) %>%
  mutate(
    Progress = as.numeric(Progress),
    Duration_s = as.numeric(`Duration (in seconds)`),
    # Age is free text in the export; one entry reads "20 years old.", which
    # as.numeric() would silently turn into NA. readr::parse_number()
    # extracts the leading number and leaves genuinely blank entries NA, so
    # demo_age$n should be 111, the full analytic sample.
    Age        = readr::parse_number(Age),
    Finished   = as.logical(Finished)
  ) %>%
  select(-`Duration (in seconds)`)

# Join the three blocks on ResponseId. `relationship = "one-to-one"` makes
# dplyr stop if a row would match more than one row; `na_matches = "never"`
# means an NA key matches nothing. ResponseId is already asserted non-NA
# above, so the second setting guards the same failure a second time.
working <- meta_block %>%
  left_join(ratings_block,   by = "ResponseId",
            relationship = "one-to-one", na_matches = "never") %>%
  left_join(responses_block, by = "ResponseId",
            relationship = "one-to-one", na_matches = "never")

# Post-join invariants. If any of these fails, the join has fabricated or
# lost records and nothing downstream can be trusted.
stopifnot(
  !anyNA(working$ResponseId),
  !any(duplicated(working$ResponseId)),
  nrow(working) == nrow(meta_block),
  nrow(working) == nrow(raw_values)
)

cat("Working frame:", nrow(working), "records x",
    ncol(working), "variables.\n")
# Expected: 119 records (117 "IP Address" + 2 "Survey Preview").
```

---

# 3. Exclusions (rules fixed before analysis)

```{r exclusions}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Exclusion rules. These rules were fixed before analysis; Study 1 was not
# prospectively preregistered. A secondary-analysis registration (2026)
# covers the joint model, maximal random effects, diagnostics and the text
# program, and states this participant flow as its fixed sample.
#
#   (0) Status == "IP Address":       real respondent records only. Qualtrics
#                                     "Survey Preview" rows are researcher
#                                     test runs (blank participant id) and
#                                     must never count as recruited.
#   (1) Finished == TRUE:             completed the full experiment.
#   (2) Seriousness == "Yes, I did":  self-reported genuine participation.
#   (3) Attention-check pass:         AttentionCheck == "Viewing images for
#                                     a set amount of time and answering
#                                     questions". The instrument (QSF, the
#                                     Qualtrics survey definition file,
#                                     question QID9) offers five options and
#                                     does not force a response. A
#                                     participant who does not choose the
#                                     correct option is shown the
#                                     instructions and the question once
#                                     more, and then continues to the
#                                     experiment whatever the second answer
#                                     is. A finished participant can
#                                     therefore have failed the check, and
#                                     the filter is a real exclusion step. On
#                                     the verified exports it drops nobody.
#
# We track the exclusion flow explicitly so the paper's participants section
# can cite exact counts at each step.
# Expected flow from the exports:
#   119 records -> (0) 117 -> (1) 114 -> (2) 111 -> (3) 111.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_exclusion_flow.csv"))

ATTN_PASS <- "Viewing images for a set amount of time and answering questions"

n_initial <- nrow(working)   # every record in the export, previews included

# Step (0): real respondent records only. Labels export codes Status as text.
stopifnot(all(working$Status %in% c("IP Address", "Survey Preview")))
after_status <- working %>% filter(Status == "IP Address")
n_status     <- nrow(after_status)
# One line per step in the knitted output, so the flow can be read off the
# report itself and not only off the CSV written below.
cat("Step (0):", n_initial, "->", n_status, "| dropped", n_initial - n_status,
    "Survey Preview / test records (Status != 'IP Address').\n")

# Participant-id invariants, asserted after the preview filter because the
# preview rows are the only legitimately blank ids. `id` is the key for
# every downstream join (long frame, NLP features, integration notebook);
# an NA or duplicated id here would silently fabricate or merge
# participants there.
stopifnot(
  !anyNA(after_status$id),
  !any(duplicated(after_status$id)),
  !anyNA(after_status$Type),
  all(after_status$Type %in% TYPE_LEVELS)
)

# Step (1)
after_finished <- after_status %>% filter(Finished == TRUE)
n_finished     <- nrow(after_finished)
cat("Step (1):", n_status, "->", n_finished, "| dropped", n_status - n_finished,
    "unfinished records (Finished != TRUE).\n")

# Step (2). NA on Seriousness typically co-occurs with Finished == FALSE; we
# treat NA as a failed-seriousness exclusion (conservative).
after_serious  <- after_finished %>%
  filter(!is.na(Seriousness) & Seriousness == "Yes, I did")
n_serious      <- nrow(after_serious)
cat("Step (2):", n_finished, "->", n_serious, "| dropped", n_finished - n_serious,
    "non-serious records (Seriousness != 'Yes, I did').\n")

# Step (3): the attention check, applied as a filter; NA counts as a fail.
after_attn <- after_serious %>%
  filter(!is.na(AttentionCheck) & AttentionCheck == ATTN_PASS)
n_attn     <- nrow(after_attn)
cat("Step (3):", n_serious, "->", n_attn, "| dropped", n_serious - n_attn,
    "attention-check failures (none on the verified exports).\n")
if (n_attn != n_serious) {
  stop(
    "Attention-check step dropped ", n_serious - n_attn, " participant(s). ",
    "The instrument lets a participant continue after a second wrong answer, ",
    "so a finished participant can fail the check, but on the verified ",
    "exports nobody does. A drop here means the export is not the one the ",
    "verified sample of 111 was built from, or the AttentionCheck column ",
    "changed. Inspect ",
    "`after_serious %>% filter(is.na(AttentionCheck) | AttentionCheck != ATTN_PASS)` ",
    "before proceeding; do NOT hardcode this step away."
  )
}

# Tabulate the exclusion flow for the paper. The table has five rows
# (initial + steps 0-3) and three columns; Study1_Supplements.Rmd and
# Study1_03_Integration.Rmd read it by filename, so any consumer that
# indexes rows by position must expect five rows.
exclusion_flow <- tribble(
  ~step,                                              ~n,         ~n_dropped,
  "Initial records in export (incl. previews)",       n_initial,  NA_integer_,
  "After (0) Status == IP Address (previews removed)",n_status,   n_initial  - n_status,
  "After (1) Finished == TRUE",                       n_finished, n_status   - n_finished,
  "After (2) Seriousness == Yes",                     n_serious,  n_finished - n_serious,
  "After (3) Attention check passed",                 n_attn,     n_serious  - n_attn
)
exclusion_flow

# Write it out for the methods section.
write_csv(exclusion_flow,
          file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_exclusion_flow.csv"))

# Adopt the final analytic sample.
dat <- after_attn %>%
  # Coerce Type to the factor order we defined in section 1.2 (Human = ref).
  mutate(Type = factor(Type, levels = TYPE_LEVELS))

# Final-sample invariants: no NA/duplicate ids, and the verified analytic
# counts. If the raw export is ever re-downloaded and these change, the
# headline results cannot be taken as the verified ones.
stopifnot(!anyNA(dat$id), !any(duplicated(dat$id)), !anyNA(dat$Type))
if (nrow(dat) != 111 || sum(dat$Type == "AI") != 55 ||
    sum(dat$Type == "Human") != 56) {
  stop("Analytic sample is not the verified N = 111 (56 Human / 55 AI): got ",
       nrow(dat), " (", sum(dat$Type == "Human"), " Human / ",
       sum(dat$Type == "AI"), " AI). Check the raw exports and the exclusion ",
       "flow above before trusting any downstream number.")
}

cat("\nFinal analytic N =", nrow(dat),
    " | AI =",    sum(dat$Type == "AI"),
    " | Human =", sum(dat$Type == "Human"), "\n")
```

### Differential attrition by condition (registered)

```{r attrition}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Differential attrition test (registered): does the rate at which
# participants leave the sample differ by condition? If the AI vignette
# made participants more likely to quit or to answer "No, I didn't" on the
# seriousness item, the two arms would keep different kinds of people and the
# comparison between them would be confounded. The table below crosses Type
# with the step at which each record left the sample, taken from the frame
# before exclusions (after step 0, i.e. every real respondent). Independence
# is tested with Fisher's exact test, which computes the probability of the
# table exactly; with counts this small the chi-square approximation is
# unreliable. Type is a Qualtrics embedded field assigned by the randomizer at
# survey start, so it exists for every real record; the code checks anyway
# and reports any NA Type.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_attrition_by_condition.csv"))

attrition_frame <- after_status %>%
  mutate(
    dropped_at = case_when(
      is.na(Finished) | Finished != TRUE                     ~ "1_unfinished",
      is.na(Seriousness) | Seriousness != "Yes, I did"       ~ "2_nonserious",
      is.na(AttentionCheck) | AttentionCheck != ATTN_PASS    ~ "3_attention",
      TRUE                                                   ~ "0_retained"
    ),
    dropped_any = dropped_at != "0_retained"
  )

n_type_na <- sum(is.na(attrition_frame$Type))
if (n_type_na > 0) {
  message("NOTE: ", n_type_na, " real record(s) have NA Type; they are ",
          "excluded from the attrition test but counted in the flow above.")
}

attrition_counts <- attrition_frame %>%
  filter(!is.na(Type)) %>%
  count(Type, dropped_at) %>%
  complete(Type, dropped_at, fill = list(n = 0L)) %>%
  arrange(dropped_at, Type)

# Test 1: dropped at any step vs retained, by Type (the question that matters).
# Test 2: the full step x Type table (shows where any difference arises).
attr_fisher_any  <- tryCatch(
  fisher.test(table(attrition_frame$Type[!is.na(attrition_frame$Type)],
                    attrition_frame$dropped_any[!is.na(attrition_frame$Type)])),
  error = function(e) NULL)
attr_fisher_step <- tryCatch(
  fisher.test(table(attrition_frame$Type[!is.na(attrition_frame$Type)],
                    attrition_frame$dropped_at[!is.na(attrition_frame$Type)])),
  error = function(e) NULL)

attrition_table <- attrition_counts %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Type, values_from = n, names_prefix = "n_") %>%
  mutate(
    n_total            = rowSums(across(starts_with("n_"))),
    fisher_p_any_drop  = if (is.null(attr_fisher_any))  NA_real_ else attr_fisher_any$p.value,
    fisher_p_by_step   = if (is.null(attr_fisher_step)) NA_real_ else attr_fisher_step$p.value,
    n_type_na          = n_type_na,
    frame              = "after step 0 (all real respondents)"
  )
attrition_table
if (!is.null(attr_fisher_any))  print(attr_fisher_any)
if (!is.null(attr_fisher_step)) print(attr_fisher_step)

write_csv(attrition_table,
          file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_attrition_by_condition.csv"))
# Expected: 6 of 117 dropped (3 unfinished + 3 non-serious); with
# counts this small Fisher p will be well above .05 unless all six sit in
# one arm. Report the counts by arm in the participants section regardless.
```

```{r demographics}

#   - age M, SD, range
#   - gender counts
#   - race counts (preserving the multi-race commas from Qualtrics)
#   - artistic-experience counts

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

                        paste0("study1_demo_",

demo_age <- dat %>%
  summarise(

  )
demo_age

demo_gender     <- dat %>% count(Gender)     %>% arrange(desc(n))
demo_race       <- dat %>% count(Race)       %>% arrange(desc(n))
demo_experience <- dat %>% count(Experience) %>% arrange(desc(n))
demo_balance    <- dat %>% count(Type)

list(
  gender     = demo_gender,

)

# Write demographics table for the paper.
write_csv(demo_age,        file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_demo_age.csv"))
write_csv(demo_gender,     file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_demo_gender.csv"))

write_csv(demo_balance,    file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_demo_balance.csv"))
```

### 3.1.1 Randomization balance table (registered)

```{r balance-table}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Covariate balance across the randomized arms (registered). `demo_balance`
# above is a condition count, not a balance test; this chunk crosses each
# demographic with Type. Randomization makes imbalance unlikely at N = 111
# but reviewers expect the table, and Study1_04_Robustness.Rmd's covariate-
# adjusted refits are only interpretable against it.
#
# Tests (one per covariate, all two-sided, with no correction for multiple
# tests, because they describe how randomization fell out and test no
# hypothesis):
#   Age         numeric        Welch t (no equal-variance assumption)
#   Gender      Female/Male/Other  Fisher exact (Other cell is n = 1)
#   Experience  ordinal 0-4    Wilcoxon rank-sum (Mann-Whitney), on ranks
#   Race        4 largest + other  Fisher exact, simulated p (B = 1e4)
# The race collapse is data-driven (four most frequent labels, everything
# else -> "Other/multiracial (collapsed)"); change RACE_TOP_K below if the
# manuscript reports a different grouping. On these exports the four most
# frequent RAW labels in the analytic sample are "Asian" (35), "White or
# Caucasian" (35), "Other" (22) and the multi-select "White or
# Caucasian,Asian" (6); "Black or African American" (4) therefore falls
# into the collapsed bucket, and the single-select "Other" (a Qualtrics
# option) is a different row from "Other/multiracial (collapsed)". If the
# manuscript reports Black participants as their own category, set
# RACE_TOP_K <- 5 or swap the frequency rule for an explicit label list;
# the test is descriptive and the choice does not touch any inferential
# result.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, c("study1_balance.csv",
                                        "study1_balance_descriptives.csv")))

EXPERIENCE_ORD <- c(
  "No formal training or experience"             = 0L,
  "A little formal training or experience"       = 1L,
  "Moderate formal training or experience"       = 2L,
  "Extensive formal training or experience"      = 3L,
  "Very extensive formal training or experience" = 4L
)
RACE_TOP_K <- 4L

balance_frame <- dat %>%
  mutate(
    gender3 = case_when(
      Gender == "Female" ~ "Female",
      Gender == "Male"   ~ "Male",
      is.na(Gender)      ~ NA_character_,
      TRUE               ~ "Other"
    ),
    experience_ord = unname(EXPERIENCE_ORD[Experience])
  )
# Stop if an Experience label appears that the map does not cover.
if (any(!is.na(balance_frame$Experience) & is.na(balance_frame$experience_ord))) {
  stop("Unmapped Experience label(s): ",
       paste(unique(balance_frame$Experience[
         !is.na(balance_frame$Experience) & is.na(balance_frame$experience_ord)]),
         collapse = " | "),
       ". Extend EXPERIENCE_ORD.")
}

race_top <- balance_frame %>% filter(!is.na(Race)) %>%
  count(Race, sort = TRUE) %>% slice_head(n = RACE_TOP_K) %>% pull(Race)
balance_frame <- balance_frame %>%
  mutate(race_collapsed = case_when(
    is.na(Race)         ~ NA_character_,
    Race %in% race_top  ~ Race,
    TRUE                ~ "Other/multiracial (collapsed)"
  ))

set.seed(20260421)   # simulated Fisher p must be reproducible
bal_age  <- t.test(Age ~ Type, data = balance_frame)
bal_gen  <- fisher.test(table(balance_frame$Type, balance_frame$gender3))
bal_exp  <- wilcox.test(experience_ord ~ Type, data = balance_frame,
                        exact = FALSE)
bal_race <- fisher.test(table(balance_frame$Type, balance_frame$race_collapsed),
                        simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 1e4)

# Per-arm descriptives to sit beside the tests.
bal_desc <- balance_frame %>%
  group_by(Type) %>%
  summarise(
    n            = n(),
    age_mean     = mean(Age, na.rm = TRUE),
    age_sd       = sd(Age,   na.rm = TRUE),
    pct_female   = 100 * mean(gender3 == "Female", na.rm = TRUE),
    exp_median   = median(experience_ord, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
bal_desc

balance_table <- tibble(
  variable  = c("Age", "Gender (Female/Male/Other)",
                "Artistic experience (ordinal 0-4)",
                paste0("Race (top ", RACE_TOP_K, " + collapsed other)")),
  test      = c("Welch t", "Fisher exact", "Wilcoxon rank-sum",
                "Fisher exact (simulated p, B = 1e4)"),
  statistic = c(unname(bal_age$statistic), NA_real_,
                unname(bal_exp$statistic), NA_real_),
  df        = c(unname(bal_age$parameter), NA_real_, NA_real_, NA_real_),
  p         = c(bal_age$p.value, bal_gen$p.value,
                bal_exp$p.value, bal_race$p.value),
  n_used    = c(sum(!is.na(balance_frame$Age)),
                sum(!is.na(balance_frame$gender3)),
                sum(!is.na(balance_frame$experience_ord)),
                sum(!is.na(balance_frame$race_collapsed))),
  levels    = c("", "Female|Male|Other",
                paste(names(EXPERIENCE_ORD), collapse = "|"),
                paste(c(race_top, "Other/multiracial (collapsed)"),
                      collapse = "|"))
)
balance_table
write_csv(balance_table, file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_balance.csv"))
write_csv(bal_desc,      file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_balance_descriptives.csv"))
```

### 3.1.2 Language (canonicalized)

```{r demo-language}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Language was collected as free text. The raw field mixes case and
# punctuation ("English", "english", "ENGLISH", "English.") that a plain
# count() splits into separate rows. Canonicalize (reduce each entry to one
# standard spelling): squish whitespace, lower-case, strip trailing
# punctuation, then title-case for display. Multi-language entries
# ("English and Mandarin", "English/Farsi") are kept as their own rows; an
# `english_any` flag captures whether English appears at all, which is what
# the text-analysis program (Study1_02_Text.ipynb) needs to know.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_demo_language.csv"))
demo_language <- dat %>%
  mutate(
    language_canonical = Language %>%
      str_squish() %>%
      str_to_lower() %>%
      str_remove_all("[.]+$") %>%
      str_squish() %>%
      str_to_title() %>%
      str_replace_all(" And ", " and "),
    english_any = str_detect(str_to_lower(coalesce(Language, "")), "english")
  ) %>%
  count(language_canonical, english_any, name = "n") %>%
  arrange(desc(n))
demo_language
cat("Participants listing English (alone or with another language):",
    sum(demo_language$n[demo_language$english_any]), "of", nrow(dat), "\n")
write_csv(demo_language, file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_demo_language.csv"))
```

# 4. Reshape to long format

```{r pivot-long}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The unit of analysis is one rating: a participant, a stimulus and a
# dimension. Qualtrics exports wide data, one column per item, and the column
# names encode the stimulus, so pivot_longer() with a names_pattern regular
# expression splits each name into its parts in one step.
#
# The regex captures three groups:
#   (\\d+)              -> stimulus number (1-5)
#   (Figure|NonFigure)  -> stimulus type
#   (Creat|Eff)         -> dimension
#
# We pivot the ratings and the response-text columns in separate passes,
# then join them on the reconstructed (id, stimulus, dimension) key.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

# --- Ratings to long ---
ratings_long <- dat %>%
  select(id, Type, Age, Gender, Race, Language, Experience,
         all_of(rating_cols)) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols          = all_of(rating_cols),
    names_to      = c("stimulus_num", "stimulus_type", "dim_short"),
    names_pattern = "^(\\d+)(Figure|NonFigure)(Creat|Eff)$",
    values_to     = "rating"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    stimulus_num  = as.integer(stimulus_num),
    dimension     = recode(dim_short, "Creat" = "creativity",
                                       "Eff"   = "effort"),
    stimulus_id   = paste0(stimulus_type, "_", stimulus_num) # "Figure_3"
  ) %>%
  select(-dim_short)

# --- Response texts to long ---
responses_long <- dat %>%
  select(id, all_of(resp_cols)) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols          = all_of(resp_cols),
    names_to      = c("stimulus_num", "stimulus_type", "dim_short"),
    names_pattern = "^(\\d+)(Figure|NonFigure)(Creat|Eff)Resp$",
    values_to     = "response_text"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    stimulus_num = as.integer(stimulus_num),
    dimension    = recode(dim_short, "Creat" = "creativity",
                                      "Eff"   = "effort")
  ) %>%
  select(id, stimulus_num, stimulus_type, dimension, response_text)

# --- Join ratings with justifications ---
long <- ratings_long %>%
  left_join(responses_long,
            by = c("id", "stimulus_num", "stimulus_type", "dimension")) %>%
  mutate(
    # Set factors with consistent orderings for all downstream analyses.
    stimulus_type = factor(stimulus_type, levels = STIMTYPE_LEVELS),
    dimension     = factor(dimension,     levels = DIM_LEVELS),
    id            = factor(id),
    stimulus_id   = factor(stimulus_id)
  ) %>%
  relocate(id, Type, stimulus_type, stimulus_num, stimulus_id,
           dimension, rating, response_text)

# Expected rows: N_participants * 10 stimuli * 2 dimensions
expected_rows <- nrow(dat) * 10 * 2
cat("Long frame:", nrow(long), "rows (expected", expected_rows, ")\n")
stopifnot(nrow(long) == expected_rows)

# Diagnostic: how many ratings are missing? Missing ratings come from
# participants who skipped items. The NA rows stay in the long frame so the
# table below can count them. Each model drops them when it filters on
# rating, so a participant who skipped an item still contributes every rating
# they did give.
missing_summary <- long %>%
  group_by(dimension) %>%
  summarise(
    n          = n(),
    n_missing  = sum(is.na(rating)),
    pct_missing = round(100 * n_missing / n, 2),
    .groups    = "drop"
  )
missing_summary
```

```{r write-long}
# It is written as UTF-8 with missing values as empty cells, which pandas

write_csv(

cat("Wrote study1_long_with_text.csv with", nrow(long), "rows.\n")
```

# 5. Descriptives

```{r descriptives}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Cell means by Condition × Stimulus Type × Dimension, averaged first within
# each participant so each participant counts equally in the cell mean; a
# participant who answered more items does not weigh more. This is the
# descriptive table for the paper.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, c("study1_cell_means.csv",
                                        "study1_marginal_means.csv")))

cell_means <- long %>%
  # Step 1: average within participant and cell, so the 5 stimuli in a cell
  # become one mean per participant.
  group_by(id, Type, stimulus_type, dimension) %>%
  summarise(participant_mean = mean(rating, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  # Step 2: summarise across participants within each cell.
  group_by(Type, stimulus_type, dimension) %>%
  summarise(
    n_participants = n(),
    mean           = mean(participant_mean, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd             = sd(  participant_mean, na.rm = TRUE),
    se             = sd / sqrt(n_participants),
    .groups        = "drop"
  )
cell_means

write_csv(cell_means,
          file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_cell_means.csv"))

# Also compute the simpler "marginal" table: ratings averaged within
# (Type × dimension), ignoring stimulus_type. This matches the two-cell
# contrast of the aggregated-t-test analyses in the earlier report (§9) and
# lets reviewers reproduce those descriptives from the analytic N.
marginal_means <- long %>%
  group_by(id, Type, dimension) %>%
  summarise(participant_mean = mean(rating, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(Type, dimension) %>%
  summarise(
    n    = n(),
    mean = mean(participant_mean, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd   = sd(  participant_mean, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
marginal_means

write_csv(marginal_means,
          file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_marginal_means.csv"))
```

# 6. Reliability of within-participant ratings

```{r reliability}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# For each dimension, check how consistent participants are across the 10
# stimuli. High reliability means a participant who rates one image as highly
# creative tends to rate the others highly too, which is what real individual
# differences (in sympathy for art, say) would produce. Low reliability would
# suggest participants were responding at random.
#
# Per-participant SDs come first (lower = more consistent), then Cronbach's
# alpha, which treats the 10 stimuli as items of one scale and measures how
# strongly the ratings move together across them.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, c("study1_reliability.csv",
                                        "study1_reliability_by_condition.csv")))

library(psych)  # for alpha(); attached for this chunk, detached at its end.

# Consistency within participant × dimension.
consistency <- long %>%
  group_by(id, dimension) %>%
  summarise(
    n_valid  = sum(!is.na(rating)),
    mean_r   = mean(rating, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_r     = sd(  rating, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups  = "drop"
  )
summary(consistency$sd_r)

# Per-dimension Cronbach's alpha across the 10 stimuli.
# The `type_name` argument lets the same function compute alpha within a
# single arm (see reliability_by_condition below). NULL = pooled across
# both arms.
alpha_for <- function(dim_name, type_name = NULL) {
  sub <- long %>% filter(dimension == dim_name)
  if (!is.null(type_name)) sub <- sub %>% filter(Type == type_name)
  mat <- sub %>%
    select(id, stimulus_id, rating) %>%
    pivot_wider(names_from = stimulus_id, values_from = rating) %>%
    select(-id) %>%
    as.matrix()
  stopifnot(ncol(mat) == 10, nrow(mat) > 2)
  # psych::alpha() handles missing ratings by using pairwise-complete data.
  # Its messages about reverse-scored items are suppressed; no item here is
  # reverse-scored.
  suppressMessages(psych::alpha(mat, check.keys = FALSE)$total$raw_alpha)
}

alpha_creativity <- alpha_for("creativity")
alpha_effort     <- alpha_for("effort")

reliability_table <- tibble(
  dimension      = c("creativity", "effort"),
  cronbach_alpha = c(alpha_creativity, alpha_effort)
)
reliability_table

write_csv(reliability_table,
          file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_reliability.csv"))

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Reliability within each arm (registered). Alpha is a ratio of
# between-person to total variance across items. When the AI arm sits ~0.9
# points below the Human arm on every item, pooling both arms counts that
# condition effect as stable between-person variance, and alpha rises for
# that reason alone. The pooled value above therefore answers "do people
# differ consistently?" partly with "yes, because we manipulated them". The
# within-arm values are the ones to report as the instrument's consistency;
# the pooled table is kept because Study1_Supplements.Rmd reads it.
# Expected: Human arm .79 (creativity) / .74 (effort), AI arm .90 / .95,
# pooled .88 / .93. So the inflation account holds for the Human arm (below
# pooled), but the AI arm is more internally consistent than the pooled
# value, not less: AI-attributed ratings are compressed toward the low end
# of the scale for every image, which raises item covariances. Report both
# within-arm values; do not write "within-arm alphas are lower than pooled"
# as a blanket statement.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
reliability_by_condition <- expand_grid(
  dimension = DIM_LEVELS,
  Type      = TYPE_LEVELS
) %>%
  mutate(
    n_participants = map2_int(dimension, Type, ~ long %>%
                                filter(dimension == .x, Type == .y) %>%
                                distinct(id) %>% nrow()),
    cronbach_alpha = map2_dbl(dimension, Type, ~ alpha_for(.x, .y))
  ) %>%
  bind_rows(
    reliability_table %>%
      mutate(Type = "pooled (inflated by condition effect; do not report)",
             n_participants = n_distinct(long$id))
  ) %>%
  relocate(dimension, Type, n_participants, cronbach_alpha)
stopifnot(!anyNA(reliability_by_condition$cronbach_alpha))
reliability_by_condition

write_csv(reliability_by_condition,
          file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_reliability_by_condition.csv"))

# Detach psych, because psych::alpha() masks ggplot2::alpha(), which the
# plotting chunks below use.
detach("package:psych", unload = TRUE)
```

# 7. Primary analyses: linear mixed-effects models

```{r lmm-helpers}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Helper that fits and reports the primary LMM for one dimension. Because it
# is one function, the creativity and effort analyses run identical code, and
# no analytic choice can have been made for one dimension and not the other.
#
# Model:
#   rating ~ Type * StimulusType + (1 | id) + (1 | stimulus_id)
#
# Rationale:
#   - Fixed effects: our two factors and their interaction (the interaction
#     tests whether the AI-vs-Human difference differs between Figure and
#     NonFigure stimuli, which would be important for reviewer concerns
#     about stimulus confounds).
#   - Random intercept for `id`: each person gets their own baseline, which
#     accounts for the 10 ratings from one person being related.
#   - Random intercept for `stimulus_id`: some images may draw higher ratings
#     than others, whatever the label.
#   - No by-participant random slope for Type. A random slope lets the effect
#     of a factor differ from one participant (or image) to the next. Type is
#     between-participant (each person sees one vignette), so there is no
#     within-person Type variation and no such slope exists.
#   - A by-stimulus random slope for Type is estimable. Type is
#     between-participant, not between-stimulus: every one of the 10 images
#     is rated by both arms (56 Human / 55 AI ratings per stimulus_id), so
#     `(1 + Type | stimulus_id)` is identified (the data can estimate it).
#     Judd, Westfall & Kenny (2012) and Barr et al. (2013) require this
#     term for the Type effect to generalize over the population of
#     stimuli rather than over these 10. The intercepts-only
#     model is the reported primary model (it is the model the headline
#     numbers come from and the one every downstream notebook consumes);
#     the fully maximal model with the by-stimulus Type slope is fit in
#     §7.5 and its by-stimulus slope SD is reported there as the direct
#     answer to the stimulus-sampling objection.
#   - The by-participant stimulus_type slope (2 levels, 5 obs per level per
#     person) is borderline-identified; it is fit in §7.4 and §7.5 as
#     sensitivity checks and is not part of the primary model. The fits that
#     carry it are singular on at least one dimension, which means at least
#     one variance or correlation in their random-effects structure sits at
#     the boundary of its range (a variance at zero or a correlation at plus
#     or minus one). It does not mean every slope variance is zero: in the
#     §7.5 fits the slope standard deviations are small but not zero, and
#     the boundary is reached by correlations at plus or minus one.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Fit status, read the same way for every lme4 fit whose numbers this file
# reports. One row with four columns:
#   fit_error      TRUE when the call stopped with an error and returned no
#                  fit.
#   converged      TRUE when the optimizer, the routine that searches for the
#                  best-fitting parameter values, reported success (return
#                  code 0) and lme4's convergence checks raised no message and no
#                  optimizer warning was recorded. The checks are the ones
#                  lmerControl() names check.conv: lme4 runs them after the
#                  fit, on the gradient (the slope of the likelihood at the
#                  solution, zero at a true optimum) and on the Hessian (the
#                  matrix of second derivatives the standard errors come
#                  from). lme4's notice of a singular fit is recorded with
#                  those messages but is not a convergence failure, so it is
#                  left out of this test.
#   singular       isSingular() at tol = 1e-4: at least one random-effect
#                  variance or correlation sits at the boundary of its range.
#   lme4_messages  every message lme4 recorded and every warning captured
#                  while fitting, joined with " | ", or "" for none.
# A reported p-value or verdict that rests on a fit with fit_error TRUE or
# converged FALSE is set to NA, and the table says why in a note column.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
lmer_fit_status <- function(fit, warnings = character(0)) {
  if (inherits(fit, "error")) {
    return(tibble(fit_error = TRUE, converged = FALSE, singular = NA,
                  lme4_messages = conditionMessage(fit)))
  }
  msgs <- c(as.character(unlist(fit@optinfo$conv$lme4$messages)),
            as.character(unlist(fit@optinfo$warnings)),
            as.character(warnings))
  failure_msgs <- msgs[!grepl("singular", msgs, ignore.case = TRUE)]
  tibble(fit_error     = FALSE,
         converged     = isTRUE(all(fit@optinfo$conv$opt == 0)) &&
                         length(failure_msgs) == 0,
         singular      = lme4::isSingular(fit, tol = 1e-4),
         lme4_messages = paste(unique(msgs), collapse = " | "))
}

# TRUE when a fit's numbers may be reported; the note says why when not.
fit_usable <- function(status) {
  !isTRUE(status$fit_error) && isTRUE(status$converged)
}
fit_note <- function(status, what = "p-value") {
  if (isTRUE(status$fit_error)) {
    paste0("fit stopped with an error, so the ", what, " is set to NA")
  } else if (!isTRUE(status$converged)) {
    paste0("fit did not converge, so the ", what, " is set to NA")
  } else ""
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The registered H1 quantity: the estimated marginal attribution contrast,
# human minus generator, averaged over the two image kinds with equal weight,
# in rating points. Under treatment coding, where each coefficient compares a
# level with the reference level (Human, NonFigure), the TypeAI coefficient is
# a different quantity, the generator-minus-human difference at non-figurative
# images only, so every check in this file that re-estimates the attribution
# effect under another model or another sample reports this contrast.
#
# df_method is passed to emmeans as lmer.df. "kenward-roger" is the
# Kenward-Roger approximation, which estimates the degrees of freedom and
# also corrects the standard errors for small samples; it is the emmeans
# default for these fits and the method behind the confirmatory family in
# section 7.9; "satterthwaite" matches the coefficient tables lmerTest prints;
# "asymptotic" skips the degrees-of-freedom computation. The estimate is the
# same under all three, and on the two primary fits so is the standard error,
# to ten decimals. NULL passes nothing, for nlme fits.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
H1_CONTRAST_LABEL <- "H1 marginal contrast: Human - AI, averaged over image kind"

h1_contrast <- function(fit, df_method = "kenward-roger") {
  emm <- if (is.null(df_method)) emmeans::emmeans(fit, ~ Type)
         else emmeans::emmeans(fit, ~ Type, lmer.df = df_method)
  pr <- pairs(emm, adjust = "none")
  s  <- as.data.frame(summary(pr))
  ci <- as.data.frame(confint(pr))
  stopifnot(nrow(s) == 1, s$contrast == "Human - AI")
  tibble(estimate = s$estimate, se = s$SE, df = s$df,
         ci_low  = if ("lower.CL" %in% names(ci)) ci$lower.CL else ci$asymp.LCL,
         ci_high = if ("upper.CL" %in% names(ci)) ci$upper.CL else ci$asymp.UCL,
         p = s$p.value)
}

fit_primary_lmm <- function(dim_name, data = long) {

  dat_sub <- data %>% filter(dimension == dim_name, !is.na(rating))

  # Set Human as reference level so coefficients read "effect of AI vs Human".
  dat_sub$Type          <- relevel(factor(dat_sub$Type),
                                   ref = "Human")
  dat_sub$stimulus_type <- relevel(factor(dat_sub$stimulus_type),
                                   ref = "NonFigure")

  fit <- lmerTest::lmer(
    rating ~ Type * stimulus_type + (1 | id) + (1 | stimulus_id),
    data    = dat_sub,
    REML    = TRUE,
    control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
  )

  # Package results into a list we can save and inspect.
  list(
    fit           = fit,
    status        = lmer_fit_status(fit),
    anova_sat     = anova(fit, type = "III", ddf = "Satterthwaite"),
    coef_table    = broom.mixed::tidy(fit, effects = "fixed", conf.int = TRUE),
    ranef_table   = broom.mixed::tidy(fit, effects = "ran_pars"),
    r2            = performance::r2(fit),
    emm_main_Type = emmeans::emmeans(fit, ~ Type),
    emm_cells     = emmeans::emmeans(fit, ~ Type | stimulus_type),
    contrasts     = pairs(emmeans::emmeans(fit, ~ Type | stimulus_type),
                          adjust = "tukey"),
    # Effect sizes in Cohen's-d units on the emmeans contrasts.
    d_cells       = emmeans::eff_size(
                      emmeans::emmeans(fit, ~ Type | stimulus_type),
                      sigma = sigma(fit), edf = df.residual(fit))
  )
}
```

## 7.3 Paper-ready stat tables

```{r tidy-stat-tables}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Flatten the creativity and effort results into two CSVs, which the
# integration notebook reads to fill in the Study 1 section of the manuscript.
# Column names are deliberately LaTeX-safe.
#
# Each row also carries its fit's status (converged, singular, fit_error,
# lme4_messages; see lmer_fit_status() in section 7) and a fit_note. If a fit
# errored or did not converge, its p-values are set to NA and fit_note says
# why.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, c("study1_lmm_fixed_effects.csv",
                                        "study1_lmm_anova.csv")))

with_status <- function(tbl, status, p_cols) {
  usable <- fit_usable(status)
  tbl <- tbl %>%
    mutate(converged     = status$converged,
           singular      = status$singular,
           fit_error     = status$fit_error,
           lme4_messages = status$lme4_messages,
           fit_note      = fit_note(status))
  if (!usable) tbl <- tbl %>% mutate(across(any_of(p_cols), ~ NA_real_))
  tbl
}

tidy_fixed <- bind_rows(
  creativity_res$coef_table %>% mutate(dimension = "creativity") %>%
    with_status(creativity_res$status, "p.value"),
  effort_res$coef_table     %>% mutate(dimension = "effort") %>%
    with_status(effort_res$status, "p.value")
) %>%
  relocate(dimension, .before = everything())

tidy_anova <- bind_rows(
  as.data.frame(creativity_res$anova_sat) %>%
    tibble::rownames_to_column("term") %>%
    mutate(dimension = "creativity") %>%
    with_status(creativity_res$status, "Pr(>F)"),
  as.data.frame(effort_res$anova_sat) %>%
    tibble::rownames_to_column("term") %>%
    mutate(dimension = "effort") %>%
    with_status(effort_res$status, "Pr(>F)")
) %>%
  relocate(dimension, term, .before = everything())
```

# 7.4 Maximal-feasible random-effects structure

```{r lmm-maximal}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# "Keep it maximal" (Barr, Levy, Scheepers, & Tily, 2013) recommends fitting
# the maximal random-effects structure the design justifies and falling back
# only when it fails to converge. For Study 1:
#
#   - Type is between-participant: no by-participant random slope possible.
#   - stimulus_type is within-participant with 2 levels: a by-participant
#     random slope is possible in principle, though with only 10
#     observations per participant, 5 NonFigure and 5 Figure, the slope is
#     only weakly estimated.
#   - Type is within-stimulus. Every stimulus is rated by participants in
#     both arms (56 Human / 55 AI per image), so a by-stimulus random slope
#     for Type is estimable and is the Judd-Westfall-Kenny term that lets
#     the Type effect generalize over stimuli. This section fits a model
#     that is maximal on the participant side only; the fully maximal model
#     that adds `(1 + Type | stimulus_id)` is fit in §7.5.
#   - stimulus_type is a stimulus-level attribute (each image is either
#     Figure or NonFigure), so it has no by-stimulus slope.
#
# So the structure fit in this section is:
#   (1 + stimulus_type | id) + (1 | stimulus_id)
# and the fully maximal structure (§7.5) is:
#   (1 + stimulus_type | id) + (1 + Type | stimulus_id)
#
# This is a sensitivity check. If it converges and the fixed-effect
# estimates match the simpler model (section 7.1/7.2), the simpler model is
# reported in the main text and convergence is noted here. bobyqa and
# Nelder-Mead are two optimizers. The fit is run with bobyqa first; if that
# fit stops with an error or is singular, it is refitted with Nelder-Mead.
# Switching optimizer does not cure a singular fit. A singular fit has at
# least one variance or correlation in its random-effects structure at the
# boundary of its range (a variance at zero, a correlation at
# plus or minus one), meaning the structure is richer than these data can pin
# down. It does not mean every slope variance is zero, so the report names the
# component at the boundary and gives the slope SDs as estimated, beside the
# fixed effects. The comparison table below carries the singular flag and the
# fit's convergence status; §7.5 does the same for the fully maximal fits.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
clear_outputs(file.path(PATH_OUT_MODELS, c("study1_lmm_creativity_maximal.rds",
                                           "study1_lmm_effort_maximal.rds")),
              file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_random_effects_comparison.csv"))

fit_maximal_lmm <- function(dim_name, data = long) {

  dat_sub <- data %>% filter(dimension == dim_name, !is.na(rating))
  dat_sub$Type          <- relevel(factor(dat_sub$Type),
                                   ref = "Human")
  dat_sub$stimulus_type <- relevel(factor(dat_sub$stimulus_type),
                                   ref = "NonFigure")

  # Try bobyqa first (our primary optimizer).
  fit_bobyqa <- tryCatch(
    lmerTest::lmer(
      rating ~ Type * stimulus_type +
               (1 + stimulus_type | id) + (1 | stimulus_id),
      data    = dat_sub,
      REML    = TRUE,
      control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa",
                            optCtrl   = list(maxfun = 2e5))
    ),
    error = function(e) e
  )

  # If bobyqa failed or produced a singular fit, try Nelder-Mead.
  if (inherits(fit_bobyqa, "error") ||
      isSingular(fit_bobyqa, tol = 1e-4)) {
    fit_nm <- tryCatch(
      lmerTest::lmer(
        rating ~ Type * stimulus_type +
                 (1 + stimulus_type | id) + (1 | stimulus_id),
        data    = dat_sub,
        REML    = TRUE,
        control = lmerControl(optimizer = "Nelder_Mead",
                              optCtrl   = list(maxfun = 2e5))
      ),
      error = function(e) e
    )
    return(list(fit = fit_nm, optimizer = "Nelder-Mead",
                bobyqa_singular = !inherits(fit_bobyqa, "error")))
  }

  list(fit = fit_bobyqa, optimizer = "bobyqa",
       bobyqa_singular = FALSE)
}

# --- Fit maximal models for both dimensions ---
max_creat <- fit_maximal_lmm("creativity")
max_eff   <- fit_maximal_lmm("effort")

# Report convergence status.
cat("=== Maximal-structure LMM: Creativity ===\n")
cat("Optimizer used:", max_creat$optimizer, "\n")
if (!inherits(max_creat$fit, "error")) {
  cat("Singular fit:", isSingular(max_creat$fit, tol = 1e-4), "\n")
  print(summary(max_creat$fit)$coefficients)
  cat("\nvs. simpler model (intercepts-only random effects):\n")
  print(creativity_res$coef_table %>%
          select(term, estimate, std.error, p.value))
} else {
  cat("Maximal fit failed:",
      conditionMessage(max_creat$fit), "\n")
}

cat("\n=== Maximal-structure LMM: Effort ===\n")
cat("Optimizer used:", max_eff$optimizer, "\n")
if (!inherits(max_eff$fit, "error")) {
  cat("Singular fit:", isSingular(max_eff$fit, tol = 1e-4), "\n")
  print(summary(max_eff$fit)$coefficients)
  cat("\nvs. simpler model (intercepts-only random effects):\n")
  print(effort_res$coef_table %>%
          select(term, estimate, std.error, p.value))
} else {
  cat("Maximal fit failed:",
      conditionMessage(max_eff$fit), "\n")
}

# Save the fits (unless they stopped with an error) for the paper's methods
# footnote on random-effects structure.
if (!inherits(max_creat$fit, "error")) {
  saveRDS(max_creat,
          file.path(PATH_OUT_MODELS, "study1_lmm_creativity_maximal.rds"))
}
if (!inherits(max_eff$fit, "error")) {
  saveRDS(max_eff,
          file.path(PATH_OUT_MODELS, "study1_lmm_effort_maximal.rds"))
}

# Build a side-by-side comparison table for the supplement.
compare_fits <- function(simple_res, max_res, dim_name) {
  if (inherits(max_res$fit, "error")) {
    return(tibble(dimension = dim_name, optimizer = max_res$optimizer,
                  fit_error = TRUE, converged = FALSE,
                  fit_note = paste("maximal fit stopped with an error:",
                                   conditionMessage(max_res$fit))))
  }
  # The registered H1 contrast is added as a last row under each structure,
  # with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom to match the coefficient rows. Its
  # sign is the reverse of the TypeAI row's (human minus generator against
  # generator minus human) and it averages over image kind where TypeAI does
  # not, so the two rows are not the same quantity.
  h1_s <- h1_contrast(simple_res$fit, "satterthwaite")
  h1_m <- h1_contrast(max_res$fit,    "satterthwaite")
  simple_fixed  <- simple_res$coef_table %>%
    select(term, est_simple = estimate, se_simple = std.error,
           p_simple = p.value) %>%
    bind_rows(tibble(term = H1_CONTRAST_LABEL, est_simple = h1_s$estimate,
                     se_simple = h1_s$se, p_simple = h1_s$p))
  maximal_fixed <- broom.mixed::tidy(max_res$fit, effects = "fixed") %>%
    select(term, est_maximal = estimate, se_maximal = std.error,
           p_maximal = p.value) %>%
    bind_rows(tibble(term = H1_CONTRAST_LABEL, est_maximal = h1_m$estimate,
                     se_maximal = h1_m$se, p_maximal = h1_m$p))
  # singular is TRUE when at least one variance or correlation in the maximal
  # fit's random-effects structure sits at the boundary of its range (a
  # random-effect variance estimated at zero, or a random-effect correlation
  # at +1 or -1): the structure is richer than the data can pin down, so the
  # supplement table carries the flag next to the estimates it qualifies.
  # The maximal fit's convergence status follows it; if that fit errored or
  # did not converge, p_maximal is set to NA and fit_note says why.
  status <- lmer_fit_status(max_res$fit)
  out <- simple_fixed %>%
    left_join(maximal_fixed, by = "term") %>%
    mutate(dimension = dim_name, optimizer = max_res$optimizer,
           singular      = status$singular,
           converged     = status$converged,
           fit_error     = status$fit_error,
           lme4_messages = status$lme4_messages,
           fit_note      = fit_note(status, "maximal-structure p-value")) %>%
    relocate(dimension, optimizer)
  if (!fit_usable(status)) out$p_maximal <- NA_real_
  out
}

re_comparison <- bind_rows(
  compare_fits(creativity_res, max_creat, "creativity"),
  compare_fits(effort_res,     max_eff,   "effort")
)
re_comparison
write_csv(re_comparison,
          file.path(PATH_OUT_TAB, "study1_random_effects_comparison.csv"))
```
